subject: Career
title: Warmth vs. Competence
description: Learn Warmth vs. Competence in one minute.

hook.text: Harvard psychologist Amy Cuddy found we judge people on two axes: warmth and competence.

buildup.text: Warmth comes first — can I trust this person? Competence follows — can they do the job?

discovery.text: Leading with competence alone makes you seem cold. Leading with warmth opens the door.

twist.text: But warmth without competence signals 'nice but not capable.' You need both in sequence.

climax.text: Start friendly and genuine. Then demonstrate your expertise. Trust first, proof second.

punchline.text: Be liked first. Be impressive second.

quiz.question: According to Amy Cuddy, which trait do people judge first?

details.summary: Social psychologists Amy Cuddy and Susan Fiske found that people evaluate others on two primary dimensions: warmth and competence. In interviews, leading with warmth builds trust, which then makes your competence claims more believable.
details.whyItMatters: Candidates who lead with competence alone often come across as cold or arrogant. Balancing warmth and competence creates the ideal impression of a capable, likable colleague.
takeaways: Warmth is judged before competence in every social interaction
Showing genuine interest in the interviewer signals warmth
Competence without warmth triggers envy rather than admiration

faq.question: How do you demonstrate warmth in a professional interview setting?
faq.answer: Active listening, remembering and referencing details the interviewer shares, smiling genuinely, and expressing authentic enthusiasm about the team or mission. Avoid performing warmth through excessive flattery, which reads as inauthentic.

faq.question: Can focusing too much on warmth make you seem less competent?
faq.answer: There is a balance point. Research shows the optimal approach is to lead with warmth to establish trust and then demonstrate competence through specific evidence. Warmth without competence creates a likable but unconvincing candidate.
